subject: optimal % of new vs. repeated sites for a multiseason/colext occupancy model?

messages.author: d3fd439c2e48caf1
messages.subject: optimal % of new vs. repeated sites for a multiseason/colext occupancy model?
parts:
Hi all, 

Can anyone recommend any papers (or otherwise offer suggestions) for how to balance a need for surveying a maximum number of sites AND have enough sites repeated over two years (to model colonization/extirpation)?  

Simplifying my scenario a bit, I  have universe of 300 sites but only enough resources to survey 100 sites per year. After randomly sampling 100 sites in year 1 (with naïve occupancy of 50%), are their general suggestions for how many new vs. previously sampled sites to sample in year 2? Should naïve occupancy in year 1 factor in decisions for where to sample repeats?

I asked a related question years ago but now I'm helping plan surveys rather than sifting through old data.

Thanks in advance!

Giancarlo

messages.author: 6ad895aa93bfdc63
messages.subject: Re: optimal % of new vs. repeated sites for a multiseason/colext occupancy model?
parts:
Hi Giancarlo,

I'll take quick crack at this (caveats apply). As far as how to allocate the effort across years at random or something, I'm not aware of any good specific guidance without understanding how one weights objectives associated with estimating dynamics vs. objectives associated with estimating psi in t=1 or 2, and the nature of the system in question. Seems like a valuable thing to consider, so could be an interesting simulation study/application.

With respect to using estimates or observations from year 1 to make sampling decision in year two, this starts to sound a bit like observations missing at non-random. Maybe something like 10.1002/eap.1754 is sensible if there are explicit sampling criteria/weights for year 2 based on year one estimates, or maybe other approaches developed to explicitly account for adaptive sampling designs make more sense. AHM V2's dynamic occupancy chapter might be a useful starting point for finding references and getting a sense of when adaptive sampling is worthwhile or not--my rough understanding is that it is most useful when random sampling is likely to produce very sparse data. 

John
